biography: Andrew Grupp writes about what people carry: fatherhood, grief, faith and its unraveling, and the daily discipline of kindness. His first book, Ash and Pine, a collection of poetry and prose, was published in 2026.

He was born in Concord, Massachusetts, and raised in South Dakota -- a New Englander on paper, a plainsman by everything since. The northern prairie, with its weather, its distances and its long winters, runs through all of his work.

He is at work on Housefall, a mythic novel about a father who loses his hall to a stranger and refuses both vengeance and disappearance on the road back to his children. The novel is coming early 2027. He lives in Nebraska.

essay.title: The Extra Hour
paragraphs: The microwave clock, glowing sickly green in the dark, stutters from 1:59 to 2:00 and there it is. The government’s Extra Hour. Handed back in the dead of night when nobody’s awake to claim it. I punch buttons to roll it back to 1:00am, then twist the dial on the analog clock, one hour backwards, the closest thing to time travel I’ll ever experience.

I’m awake. Drifting back and forth through the ancient motorhome, listening to rain drum the roof. Somewhere forward: a squat pumpkin candle, recently extinguished, smelling of smoke and autumn and dust. A cold coffeemaker. A stack of printed pages on the desk behind the passenger seat -- my novel. Thirty days of work on it starting tomorrow. A deadline I’ve been running from for a decade.
The clock reads 1:01. A minute I already lived. A minute the universe owes me.
I know the aspirational answer. Brew the good dark roast. Write. Seize the gift. Be grateful.
But the real answer is simpler and uglier.

I stand up. Cold floor. No light. I navigate by memory and green glow. The dinette light glows warm when I flip the heavy metal switch. I take down the cheap instant coffee, spoon it into a chipped mug, fill it with bottled tap water. Cold. I sit on the blue sofa and wrap my hands around it. The coffeemaker can sit idle another night.
This is my extra hour: drinking cold, shitty coffee in the dark, thinking about all the ways I’ve failed.
That’s the cruelty. An hour given back isn’t a gift; it’s an audit. A spotlight on the empty ledgers. Not time to *do, *time to *reckon*.
The clock on the wall clicks to 1:15. I sip the bitter water. I think about a girl with a laugh like wind chimes.

That’s the mercy. Permission to do nothing. For sixty minutes, I’m off the hook. Not a failure, a man in a time-out. Tomorrow, the thirty days, the novel, my whole life -- it all has to wait. It’s 1:17 am. The world is asleep. I can just… be.
1:28 am. The novel beckons. I scroll through my outline at the dinette and bravely retreat to the couch.
At 1:42 I’m tired. The real kind -- not from work, but from being my own worst company.
The click is quieter now. 1:59. Then 2:00.
It’s over. The hour is gone. The novel is still on the desk. The laptop glows, a futile summons. The coffeemaker is still cold. I’m still here. I put down the mug and walk to the aft bunk.

books.title: Ash and Pine
books.subtitle: A Collection of Prose and Poetry
description: Poems and essays from the road, the lakeshore and the long winters between. About a daughter never held and children 800 miles away. About a God who didn't show. And a fire that stayed lit anyway.

Ash and Pine: A Collection of Prose and Poetry gathers years of writing about fatherhood, grief, faith and the stubborn work of staying human when life has given you every reason to become something harder.

Across humid Tuesday nights, storm-battered camps and dark parking lots a long way from home, Andrew Grupp explores what remains when certainty falls apart -- and what we can rebuild from the pieces. These are reflections on the unraveling of old beliefs and the unexpected sacredness of ordinary things: a discount kitchen table bearing a dog's tooth marks, a diesel heater squaring its shoulders against the cold, a three-legged plastic dinosaur in an old ammo crate and the people we carry with us even when they're gone.
There are no easy answers here. No promises that suffering happens for a reason, or that everything broken will someday be made whole.

Only the conviction that kindness is a discipline. That solitude is a practice. That even in the ash, there is still an ember worth tending. And that sometimes, surviving another winter is its own quiet act of courage.
Come sit awhile. There's room beside the fire. May none cross winter left behind.

excerpts.title: Hearthwalker
lines: I am not here to save you.
I am not here to fix what broke before you found this fire.
I am here to see you. To feed you.
To make sure you know your heart is safe here.

books.title: Housefall
books.subtitle: A mythic novel
books.tagline: The hall still stands. Everything that made it a home is gone.
description: In the Northern Marches, Marek has exchanged the wars of his youth for the quiet labors of husbandry and fatherhood. Beside his wife, Roswyn, and their four children, he has built a life measured in seasons, ordinary rituals, and the familiar comforts of home.
One winter evening, a traveler arrives seeking shelter.
Housefall is a mythic novel about the uneasy distance between love and loyalty, the wounds we inflict upon those we cherish, and what remains of a life when its foundations give way.
